rv.q: Stoppard, as usual, keeps his audience perpetually on edge, unsure if we're watching a play-within-a-play or actual events unfolding, a blurring of art and life that's brilliantly mined.
What's real in Tom Stoppard's 'The Real Thing' is the exquisite pleasure of hearing his language spoken by actors who understand its music.
A terrific cast led by McGregor has triumphed with it yet again.
True to form, The Real Thing (1982) is exceedingly well made, a keen and touching study of fidelity, fiction and marital love among theater folk.

This romantic serio-comedy -- Stoppard's most accessible work -- remains a dizzying Chinese box of unpredictable devises that express devastating compassion for that most basic yet elusive human emotion.
But pretty much everything else in Sam Gold‘s hollow revival is a little off.
Out of this cat’s cradle comes a dissection of the byways of desire that finds neither Gyllenhaal nor McGregor ideally cast.
The witty word-play and posturing quickly grew tired and the characters rarely transcended their arch banter.
In this production, though, so little appears to be at stake in Henry and Annie's relationship that it does not make the crucial shift from the stage into your skull.

Despite a talented big-name cast, including the movie stars Ewan McGregor and Maggie Gyllenhaal in their Broadway debuts, this Roundabout Theater Company production is one of those unfortunate revivals that make you wonder if the play in question is worth revisiting.
This production sacrifices the pleasant strengths of The Real Thing while exposing its flaws.
That’s not too often, but only if the revivals are out of the ordinary, and Sam Gold’s lackluster staging fails to rise to the occasion.
There can be power and beauty in forthright expression, as this stirring revival reminds us.
Some people find Tom Stoppard's writing not much more than brain candy but the brilliance of this eloquent writer is his ability to go beyond the head straight to the heart.

Not only is it harder to follow the tricky plot (and its plays-within-plays), but the songs suggest a kumbaya solidarity among the characters that undercuts the show's message about the challenges of forging connections.
Ives and Claflin don't just understand their characters' mutual attraction, they feel it, and they make you feel it too.

The play concerns the complexities of marriage and marks McGregor's bang-up Broadway debut. With no sign of struggle, he's charismatic and convincing as he plays Henry's various facets -- witty, glib, snobbish and, importantly, romantic. This Scottish actor is in good company. Fellow Great White Way rookie Maggie Gyllenhaal impresses as Annie...
McGregor and Gyllenhaal hold their own against Dillane and Ehle, and offer an entirely different experience in the theater.
Mr. McGregor is lovely to watch, as he journeys through his emotional arc.
Despite the somewhat off-kilter staging, Stoppard’s dazzling wit and compassion shine through.
Though Lips Together, Teeth Apart keeps going longer than it needs to, Dubois and troupe make the ride enjoyable and thought-provoking.
Sam Gold’s production comes off as vacant and smug instead of engaging.
The actors are superb, but this is not “The real thing.”
There‘s plenty of Stoppard‘s cleverness, boxes within boxes or stories within stories, including an opening of a scene in A PLAY that you think is a scene in THE PLAY.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Stoppard revival: some praise McGregor's charismatic debut and the play's wit, but many find Gold's production emotionally distant and lacking the chemistry needed to bring this love story to life.
